chief_complaint: dyspnea on exertion, systolic murmur radiating to carotids
hpi_details: A 72-year-old female presents to the clinic with dyspnea on exertion, systolic murmur radiating to carotids. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks her breathing difficulty is due to late-onset asthma or simply the natural slowing down of old age.
concerns: She is worried she will lose her independence and be forced to move into an assisted living facility because she can no longer climb stairs.
expectations: She hopes to receive a prescription for an inhaler and vitamin supplements to restore her stamina for neighborhood walks.

investigation_events.title: Transthoracic echocardiogram
investigation_events.availability_message: The transthoracic echocardiogram report is now available.

results.value: Heavily calcified trileaflet aortic valve; peak velocity 4.2 m/s, mean gradient 44 mmHg, valve area 0.8 cm2; LVEF 57%
results.reference_range: Valve area >1.5 cm2; mean gradient <20 mmHg

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Aortic Stenosis (calcific) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes echocardiographic confirmation of severity and referral of confirmed severe symptomatic disease to a multidisciplinary valve team, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Aortic Stenosis (calcific).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Coronary artery disease without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Syncope.
management_principles: Plan for suspected aortic stenosis: obtain echocardiography; refer confirmed severe symptomatic disease to a multidisciplinary valve team for SAVR-versus-TAVR assessment
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: dyspnea on exertion, systolic murmur radiating to carotids

A 72-year-old female presents to the clinic with dyspnea on exertion, systolic murmur radiating to carotids. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Aortic Stenosis calcific.
reference_soap.assessment: Aortic stenosis is suspected from exertional dyspnea and a systolic murmur radiating to the carotids; echocardiography is required to establish severity.
reference_soap.plan: Plan for suspected aortic stenosis: obtain echocardiography. Refer confirmed severe symptomatic disease to a multidisciplinary valve team for SAVR-versus-TAVR assessment. Seek urgent evaluation for syncope, angina, or acute worsening dyspnea. Counsel patient.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Aortic Stenosis calcific
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Aortic Stenosis calcific
Implement evidence-based management plan: Echocardiogram, refer for SAVR or transcatheter TAVR

teaching.one_liner: Age-related calcification narrows the aortic valve, causing exertional breathlessness and a systolic murmur radiating to the carotids.

must_ask.say: Do you get short of breath or chest pain with activity?
How has this changed over time?
How long have you known about the heart murmur?

history.answer: Doctor, I have been getting short of breath whenever I exert myself or walk up stairs recently, and I just feel worn out.
It started about two months ago and has been gradually getting worse over the last few weeks.
I used to walk around my neighborhood without any trouble, but now I get winded after walking just one block or climbing one flight of stairs.
It has steadily progressed over time; it doesn't suddenly appear and disappear at rest, but reliably happens whenever I exert myself.
I sleep comfortably on a single pillow and haven't had trouble breathing while lying down, nor do I wake up gasping for air.
Walking up hills or carrying groceries makes it much worse, while sitting down and resting for a few minutes helps catch my breath.
No, I haven't noticed any whistling or wheezing sounds when I breathe.
No, I have had no cough, no phlegm, no chills, and no fever at all.
I sometimes feel a mild tightness in the center of my chest when I hurry, but no sharp or stabbing pain when breathing.
I felt slightly lightheaded once when walking up a steep incline, but I have never passed out or lost consciousness.
No fluttering, skipped beats, or racing heartbeat sensations; my heart seems to beat regularly.
No, I have never coughed up blood.
No swelling in my ankles or legs, and my weight has remained stable.
No swelling or tenderness in either calf, and I haven't had any recent surgery, long bed rest, flights, or hormone medications.
I have been feeling generalized fatigue and tire easily, but I haven't noticed pale skin or any dark, tarry stools.
No tingling around my mouth or in my fingers, and I haven't been feeling unusually anxious or having panic attacks.
I have never had asthma, COPD, heart attacks, or heart failure, and I do not use any inhalers.
A doctor mentioned years ago during a routine exam that I had a slight heart murmur, but they told me it was mild and didn't need treatment back then.
I worked as an elementary school teacher before retiring and never had exposure to asbestos, chemical dust, pet birds, or mold.
I do not take beta-blockers, aspirin, pain relievers, chemotherapy, amiodarone, or any medications that could cause shortness of breath.
I assumed my breathlessness was just adult-onset asthma or simply a normal part of getting older and slowing down.

I'm terrified that I won't be able to manage on my own anymore and will be forced to give up my home and move into a nursing facility. I was hoping you could give me a breathing inhaler and maybe some tonic or vitamins to get my energy back so I can walk around my neighborhood again.
My past medical history has been completely unremarkable; I have never had high blood pressure, diabetes, or kidney trouble.
I had an uncomplicated gallbladder surgery about twenty years ago, but no other operations or hospitalizations.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, vitamins, or herbal supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or materials.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products in my life.
I only drink half a glass of wine on occasional social gatherings, maybe once a month.
I am retired and live comfortably in an apartment with my husband.
Both of my parents lived into their late seventies and eighties without any early heart disease or valve problems.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, heart rate 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Alert and comfortable at rest without acute respiratory distress, cyanosis, or accessory muscle use.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor; sclerae are anicteric.
Jugular venous pressure is normal at approximately 2 cm above the sternal angle; no jugular venous distention.
Symmetric chest expansion with no chest wall tenderness or palpable heaves; apical impulse is non-displaced.
Resonant to percussion bilaterally across all lung fields.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally throughout all lung fields, with no crackles, wheezes, or rhonchi.

Harsh crescendo-decrescendo late-peaking systolic ejection murmur grade 3/6 heard loudest at the right upper sternal border radiating to both carotids; soft S2, regular rate and rhythm, with no S3 or S4.
Carotid pulses demonstrate a delayed and diminished upstroke (pulsus parvus et tardus); radial, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses are intact bilaterally.
No pretibial or pedal pitting edema on either lower extremity.
Calves are symmetric, soft, and non-tender bilaterally, with no warmth, redness, or calf asymmetry.
